targets.approach: From the Dingford Creek gate, walk or bike the closed Middle Fork road (FR 56) about 7.7 miles to its end at Hardscrabble Horse Camp; bikes go no farther. Burnt Boot stands across the Middle Fork to the south, and its north ridge drops straight from the summit to the river near 3,100 ft. There is no bridge here (the next one is at Pedro Camp, near mile 13), so head upstream from the horse camp toward Hardscrabble Creek and ford the river; it can run cold and thigh-deep in July, and logs across it may not reach. From the south bank it is cross-country up steep forest and brush on the ridge to the base of its steepest granite, where the roped climbing starts. There is no trail or established line off the valley floor.
targets.name: North Ridge

targets.approach: Reached via the North Fork Entiat Trail to Saska Basin and Saska Pass, commonly combined with ascents of Saska Peak, Emerald Peak, and Pinnacle Mountain on the same trip rather than as a dedicated single-peak approach.
targets.descent: Reverse the ridge/couloir, or descend the east/southeast slopes if that side was used to finish the climb.
targets.name: Northwest Couloir–North Ridge

targets.approach: Approached from the mountain's north side; traverse in below the summit pyramid to reach the low point on the northeast ridge before climbing the ridge itself.
targets.name: Northeast Ridge

targets.approach: Leave the Eightmile Trail onto an old logging road, then boot up an ashen, deadfall-choked burn-zone hillside for about 1,000 ft of gain. Above the burn, continue cross-country up and left toward the SE gullies, crossing a snowfield before reaching the base of the S/SE gully; expect some brief bushwhacking, loose steep dirt, and side-hilling/boulder-hopping en route.
targets.name: SE Route

targets.approach: The line most often written up starts on the Monument 78 Trail in Manning Park, BC and crosses the US/Canada border in the boundary clearing south of Castle Creek; entering the US on foot away from a port of entry is not lawful, so the lawful way in is the long walk north on the PCT from Harts Pass to Castle Pass at the head of Castle Creek. As written up, the Canadian line continues: Cross the Castle Creek bridge, push south through brush and downed timber, navigate the boundary clearing and wetland openings, then follow Castle Creek uphill from about 4,500 ft through alder terrain to a camp around 5,500 ft in Castle Creek Basin.
targets.descent: Reverse the ascent line back through the notch, northeast gully and south gully to Castle Creek Basin camp.
targets.name: South Route

targets.approach: The drive itself is easy — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek Trailhead, about 23 miles total — but the climb to Cathedral Peak is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state. From the trailhead, the Andrews Creek Trail (#504) climbs roughly 12 miles to 6,680+ ft Andrews Pass, then descends into the Spanish Creek drainage before a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lakes below the peak's southwest side, putting the one-way approach at around 18 miles with significant elevation gain and loss along the way. Most parties treat this as a 2-4 day backpack (roughly 40+ miles round trip), camping at or near Cathedral Lakes before making a summit push. A free self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead, along with a trailhead parking pass; the first many miles are a hot, rocky, buggy uphill slog with little shade, so this is genuinely a remote, multi-day alpine objective rather than a day-approach crag. For this specific route: The Monk is a distinct, smaller detached tower/buttress leaning against Cathedral Peak's south/east flank, not part of the main South Face wall. From Cathedral Lakes camp, follow the same talus slope toward Cathedral Pass but hike up into the deep gully separating Cathedral Peak from The Monk, then start on The Monk's own faces (right side of the gully); most Monk routes descend via rappels down the NE gully.
targets.descent: Descend via the NE gully, three 75-foot rappels.
targets.descent_text: Rappel the NE gully in three 75-foot (roughly 23m) rappels back to the base; a single 60m rope doubled is sufficient for each rappel.
targets.name: The Monk - Le Gibet
siblings: wa_the_monk_west_cracks_right_crack = The Monk - West Cracks - Right Crack
wa_the_monk_west_cracks_left_crack = The Monk - West Cracks - Left Crack

targets.name: The Monk - Odine

targets.name: North Ridge
siblings: wa_chimney_rock_west_face = South Peak via East Gully

wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.approach: From I-90 Exit 47, take Denny Creek Road (FR 58) about 3 miles, past Denny Creek Campground, then turn left onto FR 5830 to the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft). Follow the Denny Creek Trail (#1014, the Melakwa Lake trail) up the valley past waterfalls, then up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft above the car. At the crest of the pass turn right and follow the ridge on a bearing of about 33°, skirting cliff bands mainly on the left, to a plateau and meadow on the ridge. Early in the season, while snow still covers the brush, a brushy notch behind trees on the right leads about 170 ft up and then northeast to a meadow at the foot of the talus field that wraps about three-quarters of the peak's base; later in the season that line is choked with brush, so stay on the ridge and go straight up it to the summit block. The final scramble is loose rock on the left, or when snow-free around the exposed north side; helmets are recommended. The round trip is about 9 miles with roughly 3,600 ft of gain for Bryant alone; adding nearby Hemlock Peak makes it about 9.5 miles and 3,900 ft.
wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappels and no fixed anchors. Reverse the ascent: downclimb the loose Class 3 summit block carefully, facing in where it is steep, then return across the talus and down the ridge to Hemlock Pass, keeping to the ascent line around the cliff bands rather than cutting down the fall line. From the pass, follow the Denny Creek Trail back down to the trailhead. The steep gully between Bryant and Chair Peak on the Source Lake side is a separate line and an avalanche path in winter and spring; it is not a descent from this route.
wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.name: Southwest Ridge (Hemlock Pass)

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.approach: Park at the Dingford Creek Trailhead, where Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FS Road 56) is gated to vehicles — the last few miles of FS 56 are pitted with potholes and washboard, so high-clearance is strongly recommended — then walk or bike about 7.5 mi of closed road to its old end at the former Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead (Trail #1030). Do not follow the maintained Dutch Miller Gap trail; instead ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River roughly 300 ft upstream of the trailhead to its true-right (north) bank. Early-season and post-snowmelt (roughly June) this ford can run thigh-deep and cold — scout upstream for a braided or log crossing if flows are high. Once across, climb the boulder/talus field directly above the river for about 400 vertical feet until you hit a rock band. At the cliff, angle left (west) into a brushy gully thick with salmonberry and black currant — expect real bushwhacking here, not a trail. Follow the gully up into timber around 3,900 ft, then traverse upward through the trees until you break out onto open talus. From the talus, work up and climber's-left toward the low notch/pass beside Point 5,841, which separates Burnt Boot's summit block from the peak immediate
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the short class 3–4 ridge step off the summit block back to the Point 5,841 pass, then descend the steep snow ramp below it facing in, plunge-stepping or self-belaying with an ice axe (a controlled glissade may be possible lower down if the snow is soft and the runout is clean and known — check before committing). From the base of the ramp, work back down through talus and boulders, staying climber's-right where possible to avoid the loosest scree, drop into the timber, and downclimb the brushy salmonberry/currant gully back to the cliff band. Pick a descending line through the boulder field to the river and re-ford to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — there is no fixed rappel station or bolted anchor on this route, and the discipline (scrambling, not roped climbing) is consistent with that. In icy or wet conditions some parties might choose to build a single natural rappel (sling around a horn or tree) to protect the short class 4 step just above the pass, but that is a judgment call, not standard practice for the route. Note there is a separate, much harder roped North Ridge line on this peak (1971 first ascent by Williamson/Oas/Buch
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.name: North Route

wa_cadet_peak_scramble.approach: From the Barlow Pass trailhead (2,360 ft, pavement's end on the Mountain Loop Highway) the climb starts with roughly 4 miles of the old Monte Cristo townsite road — closed to cars, open to bikes and foot traffic — following the South Fork Sauk River to the Monte Cristo townsite (~2,800 ft); most parties bike this stretch (about an hour each way) to save legs for the scramble. Rack the bike at the bike rack under the trees in the townsite, walk through the old town, and cross the footbridge to pick up signs for the Glacier Basin Trail. The trail climbs steadily along Glacier Creek, passing a prominent waterfall (Glacier Basin Falls) before leveling into Glacier Basin proper around 4,500-5,000 ft — a good water source and, in early season, still holding patchwork snow. In the basin, find a safe spot to ford the creek (can be a wade during high snowmelt) and locate a large boulder (~15 ft) that marks the start of the scramble proper; from there head toward a second, larger boulder (~20 ft) across the basin and ascend a blown-out gully streaked reddish with old mine tailings, working up the rib between two gullies. Roughly 25 ft below a headwall with a small waterfall, exit the gully t
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.descent_text: Descend the same southwest ridge / west face line used on ascent — this is a scramble with no rappelling required (rappels: 0). From the summit block, downclimb back onto the ridge and locate the class 3 ledge that cuts back across the rock rib (it looks like a dead end at first; many parties mark it with a duck or cairn on the way up specifically to find it again on descent) — this leads back down to the loose talus traverse and around the "hobbit rock" at ~6,500 ft. Continue down the ridge to ~5,500 ft, then drop back through the brush/ledges band into the gully system. Rather than re-descending directly through the blown-out mine-tailings gully, stay skier's right to avoid steep cedar brush at the cost of a little mild bushwhacking, then rejoin the boulder landmarks back down into Glacier Basin. From the basin, re-ford the creek, retrace the Glacier Basin Trail past the waterfall to the Monte Cristo townsite, and bike/walk the old townsite road back out to Barlow Pass. Watch for loose rock and route-finding errors on the ridge/gully descent (easy to end up cliffed-out in the wrong gully), and for lingering snow/avalanche exposure on early-season descents — an ice axe (and crampo
wa_cadet_peak_scramble.name: Standard Scramble

wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.approach: From the end of FR-5606 (the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, ~3,940 ft), pick up the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437. This lower section sits outside wilderness, so mountain bikes are legal and commonly used to knock out easy miles. The first ~6 miles follow the North Fork Entiat River on a gentle, mostly forested grade, with the river itself as a reliable water source the whole way — top off here, since the route runs dry above. Some post-wildfire sections have significant blowdown; a few parties describe losing the tread briefly among downed timber and having to scramble back onto it. At about mile 6.1 a signed spur splits off to Fern Lake (Trail #1436) — stay on #1437. Around mile 7, at roughly 5,800 ft, the main trail bends sharply east and climbs switchbacks for about a half mile to a junction with the Pyramid Mountain Trail #1433 at about 6,600 ft, roughly a mile southwest of Cardinal's summit and a useful timing landmark. The final approach mile above this junction is noted as steep and loose underfoot. From the open meadow/basin past the junction, leave the trail and hike east through sparse forest, then talus, toward Cardinal's west/southwest flank. For the Southeast Slop
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.descent_text: This is a walk-down/downclimb — no rope work or anchors are needed on the Southeast Slopes line. Reverse the ascent: downclimb the loose scree gully from the notch back into the upper basin, then pick your way back down through talus and sparse forest to rejoin the North Fork Entiat Trail near the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction (~6,600 ft). From there it's a straightforward trail descent down the switchbacks to about 5,800 ft and out along the gentle lower six-plus miles back to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead. The scree gully is the main descent hazard — it's loose top to bottom, so descend deliberately, keep the group tight, and stay alert for rockfall triggered by climbers above. One trip report on this peak noted the descent taking roughly half the time of the ascent once back on established trail. No rappels are required on this route.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.name: Southeast Slopes

wa_cashmere_mountain_west_ridge.approach: From the Eightmile Lake Trailhead (~3,300 ft, reached via Icicle Creek Road and Road 7601/Eightmile Road as in the drive note), start on the Eightmile Lake Trail (Trail #1552). The trail climbs through partly burned forest and brushy slopes for about 2.8 miles to a junction just past Little Eightmile Lake (~4,400 ft) — this is the last easy water before the high country. At the junction, branch right (north) onto the Eightmile–Trout Creek Trail (Trail #1554), signed toward Lake Caroline. Follow this roughly 2.25–2.75 miles to Lake Caroline, then continue about 0.5 mile to Little Lake Caroline; both lakes sit inside the Enchantments Permit Area, so a permit is required for any overnight camping here. From Little Lake Caroline, continue about 0.8 mile toward Windy Pass (~7,220 ft). Around 6,850 ft, leave the maintained trail and head cross-country to the east, climbing gently; good bivy/camp options appear about 0.5 mile and 250 vertical feet later, around 7,100 ft — this is the last reliable water and the usual high camp for a two-day trip (strong parties push it in a single long car-to-car day, reported at up to ~17 miles round trip). From camp, climb NNE to the broad col on the we
wa_cashmere_mountain_west_ridge.descent_text: Descend by reversing the West Ridge exactly as ascended: downclimb the northwest-facing summit gully back to the ~8,200 ft contour, follow the ridge back down through the same notches/gendarmes to the 8,000 ft west col, then drop SSW back to the ~7,100 ft camp/cross-country section and rejoin the Trail #1554/Windy Pass trail. From there retrace the Eightmile–Trout Creek Trail past Lake Caroline and Little Eightmile Lake back onto Trail #1552 to the Eightmile Lake Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappels are used on the standard West Ridge route; every description of this line treats it as a reversal of the ascent. The class 3–4 sections are the main descent hazard: the ridge's loose, blocky rock and exposed ledges are more consequential to downclimb than to ascend, and it's easy to drift onto the wrong (steeper) side of the crest while trying to retrace the weaving north/south line through the notches — many parties downclimb the steepest short sections (roughly the last 50 ft below each notch) facing in, one at a time. Afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the long, open ridge and glissade-able but firm early-season snow near Windy Pass are the other things to plan around
wa_cashmere_mountain_west_ridge.name: West Ridge

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.approach: This route starts with a boat crossing of Ross Lake (Ross Lake Resort water taxi, or a private/inflatable boat carried in via the 0.6-mile portage trail from the SR-20 pullout), landing at the Lightning Creek Trailhead near the head of the lake at roughly 1,500 ft. From the shoreline, follow the Lightning Creek Trail north; parties with their own boat commonly start pre-dawn (around 4am) to leave enough daylight for the long day above, while the water taxi runs only from 8am to 5pm. After about 2 hours of hiking, watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek Trail. The first stretch above the junction is the trickiest routefinding on the whole approach: steep rock-and-alder slopes that require a rising, diagonal ascent line before you regain proper forest and trail tread — recent parties note intermittent orange flagging tape marking this stretch, which is worth watching for. Once back in the trees, tread on the Freezeout Creek Trail improves to 'decent shape' as you climb to the Freezeout Cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited immediately after a creek crossing; the cabin (maintained bunks, wood stove, logbook) is a good psychological waypoint and emergency she
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.descent_text: There is no rappelling on this route — it is a walk-off/downclimb descent that simply reverses the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the class 2-3 ground back to the notch on the southwest ridge at ~7,600 ft, then descend the same steep heather/talus/scree slope back into the Freezeout Creek drainage. This is the point where parties get into trouble: the upper basin has several gullies and chutes that look similar from above, and dropping into the wrong one risks cliffing out on bluffs well above the creek — stick to the exact ascent gully rather than improvising a shortcut. Cross back to the west side of Freezeout Creek at about 5,000 ft, follow the creek down through the old burn, rejoin the Freezeout Creek Trail tread around 4,200 ft, pass back through the cabin at 3,600 ft, and continue down to the abandoned lower Freezeout Creek Trail / Lightning Creek Trail junction, watching again for the flagged diagonal line through the steep rock-and-alder section. Finish on the Lightning Creek Trail back to the Ross Lake shoreline for the return boat/water-taxi pickup. Because of the length of the day, parties commonly finish this descent in the dark (one party that brought its own
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Standard Scramble

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.approach: The lawful approach is from the US side: cross Ross Lake by boat, follow the Lightning Creek trail and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail, then work round to the glacier below the north face. The first-ascent party instead came in from Canada — from Lightning Lake in Manning Provincial Park, BC, up and over Frosty Mountain, into Princess Creek basin, across the Princess/Crow Creek divide and down into the Crow Creek drainage — but walking into the US away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing. On that line the first-ascent party camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, about two-thirds of the way down to the approach glacier.
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.descent_text: Descend the south side of the peak and the East Ridge back toward camp; the first-ascent party described this walk-off as straightforward ('breezy'), regaining camp near twilight.
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.name: The Drawbridge

wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.approach: Same Andrews Creek/Chewuch River approach to Cathedral Pass/Upper Cathedral Lake, then toward the Cathedral-Monk gully and along the base to its left, to the open South Face.
wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.descent_text: From the summit, reverse the Southwest Route. The immediate obstacle is the long chasm that cleaves the summit rocks into north and south sections: you must cross back over it at the 'step-across', stepping onto a chockstone wedged in the slot and mantling a bulge. It is objectively an easy move with enormous exposure, and most parties belay or rig a handline with prusiks for it, especially with a rope, rack and boots on. Below that, downclimb Class 2–3 granite blocks and slabs, following ducks and cairns, and note that a 'cannonhole' further down offers an easier alternative to one vertical step on the ascent line. The angle eases into sandy slopes; drop southwest toward Cathedral Pass (7,600 ft) and pick up the trail for the last 0.6 miles to Upper Cathedral Lake. In early season the chasm can be snow-filled, which makes the first step-across trivial; late season it is bare. Allow 45 minutes camp-to-summit-to-camp on the descent and do not leave it for headlamp time.
wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.name: Last Rites

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.approach: Drive to the Andrews Creek Trailhead (~3,050 ft) at the end of West Chewuch Road/FR-51, roughly 22–23.5 miles north of Winthrop. From the trailhead, follow Andrews Creek Trail #504, which climbs steadily through the Andrews Creek drainage — the first ~6-12 miles pass through the 2003 wildfire burn scar, so expect little shade, brushy/overgrown tread in early season (some parties describe being soaked to the skin pushing through wet regrowth after rain), and occasional blowdowns despite periodic trail-crew clearing. Andrews Creek itself parallels the trail for this stretch and is a reliable water source. At about 12 miles the trail tops out at Andrews Pass (6,680+ ft), where the burn gives way to open parkland and meadow with views north toward Amphitheater Mountain; snow patches can linger here into early July. From the pass, continue on the Boundary Trail (#533) through rolling meadows, then take the Cathedral Lakes side trail (bear off near the old wilderness guard-station cabin) for the final climb to Upper Cathedral Lake — roughly 18 miles and a full, long hiking day from the trailhead. Upper Cathedral Lake is the standard base camp. From camp, cross meadows and talus toward th
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.descent_text: This is a walk-off — there is no established rappel line down the buttress, and multiple independent trip reports (2016, 2018, 2024) confirm parties descend unroped. From the summit, downclimb/scramble west and then southwest along third-class ledges on the peak's west side, aiming to regain the notch/gap system below the true summit block often called the 'summit chasm.' This gap must be crossed (or re-crossed) via an exposed step-across move above a chockstone — rated Class 4 and genuinely no-fall terrain, and the crux of the whole descent; some parties down-lead the last ~15 feet above it and place gear rather than solo it. Once across, continue down loose, blocky slopes and scree southwest, working back around the mountain's west/southwest flank to regain the meadows and talus above Upper Cathedral Lake. Total time from summit back to camp runs about 45 minutes to just over an hour for parties familiar with the line. No rope or rack beyond what's carried for the route itself is needed for a normal, dry descent — several trip reports explicitly note they carried no rappel gear and used none. Do not confuse this descent gully/notch with the SE Buttress ascent line; parties have g
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.name: Southeast Buttress

wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.approach: Base at Upper Cathedral Lake (7,380 ft). Shortest way in is the Andrews Creek Trailhead (3,050 ft) at the end of the pavement on FS 51, about 22 miles north of Winthrop: Andrews Creek Trail #504 for roughly 12 miles to Andrews Pass (6,680+ ft), descend into the Spanish Creek drainage about 2 miles to the Spanish Creek Trail junction, then take the Cathedral Lakes trail (just before the cabin, on the right) about 3 miles to the lake — roughly 17 miles and about 4,800 ft of gain. Alternatives: Chewuch River Trail #510 from Thirtymile Trailhead (3,400 ft, 29 miles up FS 51/5160), about 19.9 miles and 4,900 ft of gain on gentle valley trail; and the Boundary Trail #533 from Iron Gate (6,150 ft), about 22 miles to Cathedral Pass. From camp, the climb starts 0.6 trail miles away at Cathedral Pass.
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.descent_text: Reverse the route. The step-across is the crux in both directions and is arguably harder going down, since you are stepping onto the chockstone with the exposure in front of you rather than behind; a handline with prusiks is the standard solution and belaying it is entirely reasonable. Lower down, a cannonhole gives an easier alternative to one vertical step you may have climbed on the way up. Below the granite the ground eases into sandy slopes that plunge-step nicely; drop southwest to Cathedral Pass and pick up the trail for the last 0.6 miles to Upper Cathedral Lake. Allow about 45 minutes from summit to camp. If you have descended from a technical route on the south side, you will also traverse a talus fan and drop into the descending gully to rejoin the trail.
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.name: Southwest Route

wa_chair_bryant_traverse.approach: Begins on Chair Peak's north ridge, reached via the East Face/Northeast Buttress approach (Alpental parking, Snow Lake Trail, Source Lake fork, then a gully to roughly 4,800 ft and the basin below), then continues along the crest over/past Bryant Peak.
wa_chair_bryant_traverse.descent_text: Typically descend from wherever the traverse is exited (Bryant, the Tooth, or Denny) via that peak's own standard descent, since reversing the ridge crest is slow and exposed.
wa_chair_bryant_traverse.name: Chair-Bryant Traverse

wa_chair_peak_east_face.approach: From the Alpental parking lot, take the Snow Lake Trail; at about 1.5 miles turn off toward Source Lake. Ascend a 3rd-class rocky gully starting around 4,200 ft, reach a small cliff around 4,800 ft, traverse through a notch, then cross a snowy basin to the base of the route around 5,500 ft.
wa_chair_peak_east_face.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb and traverse back toward the notch area, locate the marked south-facing rappel gully (the southern chimney), and make two single-rope rappels down the chimney and a third down the steep, narrow snow finger below it to return to the approach basin.
wa_chair_peak_east_face.name: East Face

wa_chair_peak_north_face.approach: Park at the upper Alpental parking lot (end of Alpental Road, shared with the Snow Lake / Source Lake trailhead). Pick up the maintained Alpental Valley trail, which runs along and above the South Fork Snoqualmie River on the old ski-area service road/cat track for about the first 0.5 mile before narrowing to a standard trail. Continue up-valley roughly 1.5-2 miles, climbing gently through forest and avalanche-path brush with Chair Peak's north side visible ahead; a boot path forks off the main Source Lake/Snow Lake trail toward Source Lake and the basin below Chair Peak's east/north aspect (~4200 ft). From the basin, ascend talus and (in season) a snow apron directly toward the base of the north face at the head of the Alpental cirque, aiming for the obvious snow/ice runnel system below the summit block. Total approach gain to the base is roughly 2,400 ft over about 2.5-3 miles one-way. Hazards: the valley floor and lower slopes cross active avalanche paths below Chair Peak, Snoqualmie Mountain, and The Tooth, so this is a serious slide-prone approach in winter/spring — most parties go early and move quickly through the runout zones; there is also a creek crossing near Source Lake
wa_chair_peak_north_face.descent_text: From the summit, most parties reverse toward the notch/col below the summit block and descend the gully on the south side of the east face (sometimes described as the same gully used by the Northeast Buttress descent). Expect a mix of downclimbing and rappelling: parties commonly do two double-rope (60m) rappels — the first from trees/rock anchors near the head of the gully with some downclimbing to reach the next station, and a second double-rope rappel that reaches easier snow near the gully's base — though some parties describe reaching the base with a single 60m rappel plus downclimbing depending on snow coverage. Anchors are a mix of natural gear (trees, rock horns/slings) rather than bolts; bring cord/webbing to back up or replace tattered slings. From the base of the gully, downclimb snow/talus east back into the Chair Peak basin and pick up the approach trail to Source Lake and out. Watch for cornices at the gully lip early season, loose rock in the gully when snow-free, and wet-slide hazard on the descent slopes during warm spring conditions.
wa_chair_peak_north_face.name: North Face

wa_chair_peak_northeast_buttress.approach: From the upper Alpental parking lot (I-90 Exit 52, end of Alpental Road), follow the Alpental Valley/Source Lake trail: the first 0.5 mile follows the old ski-area cat track, then it becomes a standard trail climbing gently through forest for about 0.75 mile to Source Lake (roughly 1.25-1.75 miles and a few hundred feet of gain from the car). From Source Lake, leave the maintained trail and head cross-country/up boot path toward the basin below Chair Peak's east face (~4200 ft), a further 0.5-1 mile with steeper talus, heather, and (early/mid season) snow slopes. From the basin, climb a short snow gully for approximately 300 ft to gain the crest of the ridge that forms the Northeast Buttress, then follow the ridge to the start of the technical climbing. Total approach is on the order of 2-2.5 miles and 1,700-2,000 ft of gain one-way to the base of the buttress. Hazards: the basin and approach gully sit below avalanche terrain off Chair Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain — this is a classic early-season slide path, and parties often describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity, and wind-loaded slopes here; a rope/axe/crampons are typically carried from the basin onward given the exposure o
wa_chair_peak_northeast_buttress.descent_text:
From the top of the buttress, scramble back across the flat summit area and drop into the first obvious gully on climber's left — not the gully further along the ridge near the true summit. Old tat on two small trees marks the entrance. The gully runs due south between high rock walls: scramble down it and take the very first left it offers, and the rappel station comes into view as soon as the walls let you out, at roughly 6,000 ft. Parties miss it by carrying on too far down, or too far right, once the gully opens up.

The station is fixed and old — three rusty pitons tied together with a mass of aging webbing and a pair of aluminium rappel rings. Two ropes give a single 60 m rappel that clears the corniced lip and lands where the gully opens out and ends; a single 60 m rope halves that and leaves 30-40 m of very steep snow to downclimb, still fully exposed to whatever comes down the gully. Move to the side of the gully mouth once you are down so the next person cannot drop anything on you. A tag line is worth carrying for exactly that reason — it buys a quick rappel to a protected stance instead of a long spell standing in the fall line.

wa_chair_peak_northeast_buttress.name: Northeast Buttress

wa_chair_peak_northwest_ridge.approach: Follow the East Face approach to the 'Thumbtack Rock' landmark, then head right up a grassy gully over the ridge toward the start of the Northwest Ridge.
wa_chair_peak_northwest_ridge.descent_text: From the true summit, traverse south across a series of false summits until reaching a tree rigged with rappel anchors at the second gully encountered heading east. Make multiple rappels down this gully to reach the East Face proper, then descend scree slopes back to Thumbtack Rock and the standard approach path.
wa_chair_peak_northwest_ridge.name: Northwest Ridge

wa_chair_peak_west_ridge.approach: From the Alpental lot, follow the standard Northeast Buttress approach to the base of that buttress, then keep traversing west beneath the north face on slabby terrain that can be snowy and glide-cracked in early season to reach the base of the route, roughly 2-2.5 hours from the parking area.
wa_chair_peak_west_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, descend via the standard south-side couloir, which funnels into the same narrow rappel gully used by the other Chair Peak routes; reported descent time is about 1-2 hours back to the Chair Peak basin.
wa_chair_peak_west_ridge.name: West Ridge

wa_chimney_rock_east_face_direct.approach: Same as the standard East Face: Pete Lake Trailhead (2,800 ft) via Pete Lake Trail/PCT and the Chimney Creek climber's path to high camp at Sunrise Knob (~4,600-4,800 ft).
wa_chimney_rock_east_face_direct.descent_text: Once the route rejoins the standard East Face partway up, descend as for that route: downclimb/rappel with a single rope, carrying spare webbing for old anchors.
wa_chimney_rock_east_face_direct.name: East Face Direct

wa_chimney_rock_west_face.approach: This route shares the same trailhead-to-basin approach as the East Face: from the Pete Lake Trailhead off FR 4616, hike the Pete Lake Trail #1323 (~4 easy miles to Pete Lake, then ~2 more miles) to the Pacific Crest Trail junction, head north on the PCT about a mile to the Chimney Creek avalanche-path crossing, then leave the PCT and follow the climber's path (flagged/cairned, fords Chimney Creek and crosses several brushy ravines) up through Sunrise Knob (~4,650 ft, ~4-5 hrs from the trailhead) to the moraine and the bivy basin at the toe of the Chimney Glacier (~5,400 ft) — see the East Face route's approach text for full turn-by-turn detail on this shared stretch, and treat it as a 2-3 day car-to-car trip. Above camp, a wet, grubby gully through the rock band leads onto the upper Chimney Glacier; rope up, cross toward the gully below the notch between the central and south summits, and be ready to improvise around the moat at the foot of the rock, which gets worse later in the season. Water and camping options match the East Face approach: Pete Lake, the low Chimney Creek crossings, or melted glacier snow above the moraine.
wa_chimney_rock_west_face.descent_text: Descend the line of ascent. From the South Peak, return about 400 ft to the notch between the central and south summits, then follow the ledge system back down; the ledges are easy to pick out from above. Rappel the steeper, wet fourth-class steps on a single 60 m rope rather than downclimbing them. No fixed anchors are known on this line, so carry slings, cord and a few rap rings to build and leave your own. Cross the moat back onto the glacier, reverse the glacier and the gully through the rock band, and return to camp.
wa_chimney_rock_west_face.name: South Peak via East Gully

wa_east_face_6.approach: From the Pete Lake Trailhead off FR 4616 (elev. ~2,850 ft), follow the Pete Lake Trail #1323 west and north through open, nearly-flat forest along Cooper River/Lemah Meadow terrain — easy tread and wildflower meadows for about 4 miles to the south shore of Pete Lake, a popular first camp and reliable water source. Continue past the lake about a mile, through Lemah Meadow, to the Pacific Crest Trail junction and turn north onto the PCT. After about a mile of PCT travel, watch for a wide avalanche path with heavy blowdown crossing the trail near the confluence of Chimney Creek — this is the turnoff for the climb. Leave the PCT and work climber's-right across the avalanche debris to pick up a boot/climber's path on the true-right side of Chimney Creek (it starts roughly 20 yards inside the timber at an obvious logjam that serves as the creek crossing, and is marked intermittently with orange flagging and cairns). The path crosses three brushy ravines, and pushes through alder and vine maple before breaking into open moraine and a hanging basin — cairns mark the line through this stretch, which is the main route-finding crux of the approach. wa_east_face_6.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line rather than continuing over the summit block. From the summit, rappel the three summit pitches back to the broad ledge below the tower (two rappels on a single rope; some parties make three), then traverse back through the notch/gully between the main and south summits (a short reversal of the ascent gully, Class 3-4 downclimbing over loose debris or snow/ice depending on season). Where the rock steepens near the base of the face, on the wet, lower-angle slabs just above the glacier, most parties make two rappels over these fourth-class steps using a single rope (a 50-60m/165ft rope is enough for each); anchors here are natural — slung horns and blocks rather than bolts — so carry cord/webbing to back up or replace old tat, especially early in the season. Below the raps, a final short third-class downclimb regains the bergschrund/moat crossing back onto the Chimney Glacier, then reverse the moraine and climber's path to Sunrise Knob and the Pete Lake Trail. Watch for loose rock/rockfall in the gully, wet slick rock on the fourth-class rappel steps, and crevasse/moat hazard back on the glacier.
wa_east_face_6.name: East Face

wa_ne_ridge.approach: The drive itself is easy — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek Trailhead, about 28 miles total — but the climb to Cathedral Peak is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state. From the trailhead, the Andrews Creek Trail (#504) climbs roughly 12 miles to 6,680+ ft Andrews Pass, then descends into the Spanish Creek drainage before a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lakes below the peak's southwest side, putting the one-way approach at around 18 miles with significant elevation gain and loss along the way. Most parties treat this as a 2-4 day backpack (roughly 40+ miles round trip), camping at or near Cathedral Lakes before making a summit push. A free self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead, along with a trailhead parking pass; the first many miles are a hot, rocky, buggy uphill slog with little shade, so this is genuinely a remote, multi-day alpine objective rather than a day-approach crag. wa_ne_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb/walk off to the west along the regular walk-up (SW slope) descent route used by all Cathedral Peak climbs; a short rappel may help getting off the summit ridge itself.
wa_ne_ridge.name: NE Ridge

wa_north_face_left_buttress.approach: Two approaches exist, both multi-day. The first-ascent party came from Canada: from Lightning Lake in E.C. Manning Provincial Park, about seven miles of trail over the Frosty Mountain area to a pass near 8,000 ft, then cross-country south over the border, through the Princess Creek basin and into the Crow Creek drainage below Castle's north face to the toe of the north-face glacier. Walking into the US away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing, so that line is recorded, not recommended. The lawful approach is from the US side: boat or hike up Ross Lake from the WA-20/Ross Dam trailhead (permit from the North Cascades Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount) to Lightning Creek, then follow the Lightning Creek Trail and the abandoned, increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek Trail past the Freezeout cabin (3,600 ft), a much longer multi-day trudge. Both approaches finish by crossing the mellow north-face glacier to the base of the buttress -- watch for an awkward bergschrund/moat at the start of the route.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.descent_text: From the top of the route, descend via Castle Peak's east ridge to an obvious col, then down a snow finger back toward the approach glacier/basin, rather than reversing the climbing line.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Fight or Flight

wa_south_face_10.descent_text: Descend west off the summit via the regular class-3 walk-up route, the same descent used by the NE Ridge route; involves loose talus and some downclimbing back toward camp.
wa_south_face_10.name: South Face

wa_the_monk_scabo.descent_text: Rappel the NE gully in three 75-foot (roughly 23m) rappels back to the base.

wa_the_monk_west_cracks_left_crack.descent_text: Short enough to rappel the route on gear from the top of the second pitch. If you link into the upper formation and top out on The Monk, descend the northeast gully with three 75-foot rappels — a doubled 60 m rope covers each. Carry webbing and rings; the anchors are not documented as fixed. From the base, walk down the talus and slabs to the drainage and back to Upper Cathedral Lake in 30–40 minutes.
